**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

content.content:
1	# wal-store
2	
3	Key value store that appends every mutation to a write-ahead log first, so a process killed between writes and checkpoints recovers exactly the committed state.
4	
5	## Requirements
6	
7	Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only.
8	
9	## Install
10	
11	    python3 -m pip install -e .
12	
13	## Run
14	
15	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store recover
16	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store put <key> --value-file <path>
17	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store get <key>
18	
19	## Public interface
20	
21	`wal_store.Store(path)` opens the store directory. The directory must
22	exist; opening a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` (the `put` command
23	line subcommand creates it).
24	- `put(key, value) -> None` records a mutation.
25	- `get(key) -> bytes | None` reads the value at the last committed snapshot.
26	- `delete(key) -> None` records a removal.
27	- `delete_range(start=None, end=None) -> None` records a batch removal of
28	  every committed key in a half-open byte range (`delete(start, end)` is
29	  the same call).
30	- `commit() -> int` advances the durable sequence number. Every call writes
31	  a commit marker and advances the sequence by exactly one, including a
32	  commit with no pending changes; the first commit after a compaction is the
33	  pre-compaction sequence plus one.
34	- `recover() -> dict` replays the log and reports what it applied.
35	- `compact() -> dict` rewrites committed history into one tight log and
36	  reclaims the old space, without changing the committed state or the
37	  durable sequence.
38	- `scan(start=None, end=None) -> ScanCursor` opens an ordered read-only
39	  cursor over the committed snapshot pinned at that moment.
40	- `ScanCursor.token() -> bytes` (alias `mark()`) serialises the cursor's
41	  current position into a resumable scan token; `scan(token=tok)`
42	  (alias `scan(resume=tok)`) continues that scan from the token.
43	- `stats() -> dict` reports sequence, entries and bytes.
44	
45	## Scanning
46	
47	`scan()` works on both open forms and never touches the write path. The
48	returned cursor is an iterator of `(key, value)` pairs in bytewise key
49	order — keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes and values come back as the
50	exact stored bytes, with no encoding conversion — covering `start`
51	inclusive through `end` exclusive; a `None` endpoint leaves that side
52	unbounded, so `scan()` walks everything. Keys that only ever appeared in
53	delete records never show up, a key overwritten any number of times yields
54	only its last committed value, and empty values scan like any other. A
55	writer's uncommitted changes are not part of the snapshot — they are
56	invisible to `scan()` and to `get()` alike, both of which read the last
57	committed snapshot; a read-only store scans the snapshot it pinned at open.
58	
59	The snapshot is materialised once when the cursor opens, so later commits,
60	compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space never
61	change what the cursor yields, and the same snapshot scans to the identical
62	sequence before and after compaction. Scanning never replays the log,
63	takes no lock and keeps no history in memory, so its cost is independent
64	of the log's length. A `start` that sorts after `end` raises `ValueError`,
65	as does reading from a cursor after `close()` (the cursor is also a
66	context manager).
67	
68	## Resumable scans
69	
70	A scan can be paused and later continued from exactly where it stopped, in
71	the same process or after reopening the store (writer or read-only). At any
72	point a cursor can serialise its current position into an opaque `bytes`
73	token:
74	
75	- `ScanCursor.token()` returns the token; `mark()` is an alias.
76	- `Store.scan(token=tok)` opens a new cursor that continues the identical
77	  range from the identical position over the identical snapshot;
78	  `scan(resume=tok)` is an alias. The token already carries its range, so
79	  passing `start`/`end` together with a token raises `ValueError`.
80	
81	Splitting one scan at a token and concatenating the pieces yields exactly
82	the pairs a single uninterrupted scan would have yielded, byte for byte:
83	the resumed stream is the tail of the original scan.
84	
85	The token names the snapshot it pins — the durable sequence number and a
86	content identity over the snapshot's canonical image — together with the
87	scan range and the next position. It stays valid across later commits,
88	compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space. When a
89	writer mints a token it durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an
90	immutable, content-addressed `wal.s<seq>.<id>` sidecar (an atomic write,
91	never edited in place), so the token keeps resolving after the underlying
92	log bytes are compacted away; snapshots that were never published can also
93	be reconstructed from the committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A
94	read-only store never creates or modifies a file, even when minting a
95	token; such a token still resolves because the writer has published (or can
96	reconstruct) that snapshot.
97	
98	Deleted keys never come back. A token pins one exact committed snapshot:
99	resuming it reads precisely that snapshot, whether or not the same keys were
100	later deleted, and a range tombstone that compaction has since reclaimed
101	neither removes nor revives anything on the resumed path. A fresh scan of a
102	snapshot after the delete never shows the key.
103	
104	A token is opaque and strictly validated. Anything forged, truncated,
105	corrupted (checksum mismatch), carrying an out-of-range position, naming a
106	reversed range, or referring to a snapshot this store does not hold (a
107	foreign store, or a snapshot whose every copy has been reclaimed) raises
108	`ValueError`; nothing is guessed or repaired. A non-`bytes` token raises
109	`TypeError`. The token format is platform-independent: the same snapshot at
110	the same position always mints byte-identical tokens on Windows and Linux
111	(all integers are big-endian and no bytes are translated), so tokens can be
112	handed across platforms and processes.
113	
114	
115	## Range deletes
116	
117	`delete_range(start=None, end=None)` removes every committed key a scan
118	of the same endpoints would return: keys compare by their raw UTF-8
119	bytes, the range is half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive) and a
120	`None` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so `delete_range()` clears
121	the whole store while `delete_range("a", "a")` removes nothing. The
122	shorthand `delete(start, end)` is the same call; `delete(key)` still
123	removes one key. Endpoint validation is shared with `scan`: non-string
124	endpoints raise `TypeError` and a `start` sorting after `end` raises
125	`ValueError`.
126	
127	Like every other mutation the tombstone is only staged in the session:
128	it is invisible to scans and read-only stores until `commit()`, and a
129	writer that is killed first reopens at the last committed state. Once
130	committed, the covered keys disappear from single-key reads and scans
131	alike, and a key that only ever appears in delete history can never come
132	back. Writing a key inside a previously deleted range simply stores the
133	new value — after commit it reads back as that last committed value,
134	with keys and values still handled as raw bytes.
135	
136	Recovery resolves a range tombstone by removing the covered keys; the
137	report counts the tombstone record under `applied`. Compaction reclaims
138	it together with the rest of the dead history: the compacted image
139	contains one live put per surviving key and no tombstones at all, so
140	reclaiming the record can never resurrect a deleted key, and a snapshot
141	scans to the identical bytes before and after compaction.
142	
143	## Read-only stores
144	
145	`wal_store.Store(path, read_only=True)` opens an isolated reader. Any
146	number of read-only processes may coexist with the single writer in the
147	same directory. A reader takes no lock and never creates or changes a
148	file; it pins a snapshot at open time and every `get` reads from that one
149	complete committed snapshot, so uncommitted mutations, a half-written
150	commit, a torn record or a half-finished shrink are never visible.
151	Successive reads from the same reader may advance across snapshots only by
152	reopening; each read is of one fully committed snapshot. Reads do not
153	replay the log and do not block the writer: killing or suspending a reader
154	never affects the writer's commits, recovery or stats. `put`, `delete`,
155	`commit` and `recover` are rejected on a read-only store; `stats` reports
156	the pinned snapshot and `get` is the normal way to read it. Readers serve
157	from the atomically replaced `wal.ckp` sidecar (and the committed log
158	prefix), so directories written by older versions open directly.
159	
160	`wal_store.inject_tear(source, destination, offset)` is a verification aid:
161	it writes a byte-for-byte copy of `source` cut at exactly `offset` bytes (a
162	replica of a process killed at that write position) to `destination` and
163	leaves the source untouched. Either argument may be a store directory, in
164	which case its `wal.log` is used. A negative or past-the-end offset raises
165	`IndexError`. It is never used by the normal write path.
166	
167	## Recovery
168	
169	`recover()` returns a report with three integer fields, in this key order:
170	
171	- `applied` — committed put/delete records replayed into the state,
172	- `discarded` — torn tail records dropped (at most one, the unfinished final
173	  write left by a process killed mid append; `0` on a clean log),
174	- `seq` — the durable sequence number after recovery.
175	
176	A record killed halfway through is not a mutation: it is discarded and the
177	recovered state is exactly the last committed state. An empty log recovers
178	to an empty state, which is a normal result. Recovery truncates the dirty
179	tail and the next commit uses `seq + 1`, no matter how often the store is
180	reopened.
181	
182	### Recovery may itself be killed
183	
184	Recovery is an idempotent, kill-safe convergence. Interrupting it at any
185	point — while the dirty tail is being dropped or the log is being rebuilt —
186	and reopening any number of times reaches exactly the state and the report
187	of one clean recovery, with exit code `0`; the durable sequence never
188	regresses and the next commit is always `seq + 1`.
189	
190	Two internal sidecar files in the store directory make this work; they are

# wal-store

Key value store that appends every mutation to a write-ahead log first, so a process killed between writes and checkpoints recovers exactly the committed state.

## Requirements

Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only.

## Install

    python3 -m pip install -e .

## Run

    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store recover
    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store put <key> --value-file <path>
    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store get <key>

## Public interface

`wal_store.Store(path)` opens the store directory. The directory must
exist; opening a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` (the `put` command
line subcommand creates it).
- `put(key, value) -> None` records a mutation.
- `get(key) -> bytes | None` reads the value at the last committed snapshot.
- `delete(key) -> None` records a removal.
- `delete_range(start=None, end=None) -> None` records a batch removal of
  every committed key in a half-open byte range (`delete(start, end)` is
  the same call).
- `commit() -> int` advances the durable sequence number. Every call writes
  a commit marker and advances the sequence by exactly one, including a
  commit with no pending changes; the first commit after a compaction is the
  pre-compaction sequence plus one.
- `recover() -> dict` replays the log and reports what it applied.
- `compact() -> dict` rewrites committed history into one tight log and
  reclaims the old space, without changing the committed state or the
  durable sequence.
- `scan(start=None, end=None) -> ScanCursor` opens an ordered read-only
  cursor over the committed snapshot pinned at that moment.
- `ScanCursor.token() -> bytes` (alias `mark()`) serialises the cursor's
  current position into a resumable scan token; `scan(token=tok)`
  (alias `scan(resume=tok)`) continues that scan from the token.
- `stats() -> dict` reports sequence, entries and bytes.

## Scanning

`scan()` works on both open forms and never touches the write path. The
returned cursor is an iterator of `(key, value)` pairs in bytewise key
order — keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes and values come back as the
exact stored bytes, with no encoding conversion — covering `start`
inclusive through `end` exclusive; a `None` endpoint leaves that side
unbounded, so `scan()` walks everything. Keys that only ever appeared in
delete records never show up, a key overwritten any number of times yields
only its last committed value, and empty values scan like any other. A
writer's uncommitted changes are not part of the snapshot — they are
invisible to `scan()` and to `get()` alike, both of which read the last
committed snapshot; a read-only store scans the snapshot it pinned at open.

The snapshot is materialised once when the cursor opens, so later commits,
compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space never
change what the cursor yields, and the same snapshot scans to the identical
sequence before and after compaction. Scanning never replays the log,
takes no lock and keeps no history in memory, so its cost is independent
of the log's length. A `start` that sorts after `end` raises `ValueError`,
as does reading from a cursor after `close()` (the cursor is also a
context manager).

## Resumable scans

A scan can be paused and later continued from exactly where it stopped, in
the same process or after reopening the store (writer or read-only). At any
point a cursor can serialise its current position into an opaque `bytes`
token:

- `ScanCursor.token()` returns the token; `mark()` is an alias.
- `Store.scan(token=tok)` opens a new cursor that continues the identical
  range from the identical position over the identical snapshot;
  `scan(resume=tok)` is an alias. The token already carries its range, so
  passing `start`/`end` together with a token raises `ValueError`.

Splitting one scan at a token and concatenating the pieces yields exactly
the pairs a single uninterrupted scan would have yielded, byte for byte:
the resumed stream is the tail of the original scan.

The token names the snapshot it pins — the durable sequence number and a
content identity over the snapshot's canonical image — together with the
scan range and the next position. It stays valid across later commits,
compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space. When a
writer mints a token it durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an
immutable, content-addressed `wal.s<seq>.<id>` sidecar (an atomic write,
never edited in place), so the token keeps resolving after the underlying
log bytes are compacted away; snapshots that were never published can also
be reconstructed from the committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A
read-only store never creates or modifies a file, even when minting a
token; such a token still resolves because the writer has published (or can
reconstruct) that snapshot.

Deleted keys never come back. A token pins one exact committed snapshot:
resuming it reads precisely that snapshot, whether or not the same keys were
later deleted, and a range tombstone that compaction has since reclaimed
neither removes nor revives anything on the resumed path. A fresh scan of a
snapshot after the delete never shows the key.

A token is opaque and strictly validated. Anything forged, truncated,
corrupted (checksum mismatch), carrying an out-of-range position, naming a
reversed range, or referring to a snapshot this store does not hold (a
foreign store, or a snapshot whose every copy has been reclaimed) raises
`ValueError`; nothing is guessed or repaired. A non-`bytes` token raises
`TypeError`. The token format is platform-independent: the same snapshot at
the same position always mints byte-identical tokens on Windows and Linux
(all integers are big-endian and no bytes are translated), so tokens can be
handed across platforms and processes.


## Range deletes

`delete_range(start=None, end=None)` removes every committed key a scan
of the same endpoints would return: keys compare by their raw UTF-8
bytes, the range is half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive) and a
`None` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so `delete_range()` clears
the whole store while `delete_range("a", "a")` removes nothing. The
shorthand `delete(start, end)` is the same call; `delete(key)` still
removes one key. Endpoint validation is shared with `scan`: non-string
endpoints raise `TypeError` and a `start` sorting after `end` raises
`ValueError`.

Like every other mutation the tombstone is only staged in the session:
it is invisible to scans and read-only stores until `commit()`, and a
writer that is killed first reopens at the last committed state. Once
committed, the covered keys disappear from single-key reads and scans
alike, and a key that only ever appears in delete history can never come
back. Writing a key inside a previously deleted range simply stores the
new value — after commit it reads back as that last committed value,
with keys and values still handled as raw bytes.

Recovery resolves a range tombstone by removing the covered keys; the
report counts the tombstone record under `applied`. Compaction reclaims
it together with the rest of the dead history: the compacted image
contains one live put per surviving key and no tombstones at all, so
reclaiming the record can never resurrect a deleted key, and a snapshot
scans to the identical bytes before and after compaction.

## Read-only stores

`wal_store.Store(path, read_only=True)` opens an isolated reader. Any
number of read-only processes may coexist with the single writer in the
same directory. A reader takes no lock and never creates or changes a
file; it pins a snapshot at open time and every `get` reads from that one
complete committed snapshot, so uncommitted mutations, a half-written
commit, a torn record or a half-finished shrink are never visible.
Successive reads from the same reader may advance across snapshots only by
reopening; each read is of one fully committed snapshot. Reads do not
replay the log and do not block the writer: killing or suspending a reader
never affects the writer's commits, recovery or stats. `put`, `delete`,
`commit` and `recover` are rejected on a read-only store; `stats` reports
the pinned snapshot and `get` is the normal way to read it. Readers serve
from the atomically replaced `wal.ckp` sidecar (and the committed log
prefix), so directories written by older versions open directly.

`wal_store.inject_tear(source, destination, offset)` is a verification aid:
it writes a byte-for-byte copy of `source` cut at exactly `offset` bytes (a
replica of a process killed at that write position) to `destination` and
leaves the source untouched. Either argument may be a store directory, in
which case its `wal.log` is used. A negative or past-the-end offset raises
`IndexError`. It is never used by the normal write path.

## Recovery

`recover()` returns a report with three integer fields, in this key order:

- `applied` — committed put/delete records replayed into the state,
- `discarded` — torn tail records dropped (at most one, the unfinished final
  write left by a process killed mid append; `0` on a clean log),
- `seq` — the durable sequence number after recovery.

A record killed halfway through is not a mutation: it is discarded and the
recovered state is exactly the last committed state. An empty log recovers
to an empty state, which is a normal result. Recovery truncates the dirty
tail and the next commit uses `seq + 1`, no matter how often the store is
reopened.

### Recovery may itself be killed

Recovery is an idempotent, kill-safe convergence. Interrupting it at any
point — while the dirty tail is being dropped or the log is being rebuilt —
and reopening any number of times reaches exactly the state and the report
of one clean recovery, with exit code `0`; the durable sequence never
regresses and the next commit is always `seq + 1`.

Two internal sidecar files in the store directory make this work; they are
not part of the public API and are maintained entirely below the write
path:

- `wal.ckp` is an atomically replaced copy of the log prefix ending at the
  most recent commit marker. A log torn at *any* offset — even offset 0, or
  inside the committed prefix — is silently rebuilt from it, so a
  half-finished convergence can never be mistaken for a torn tail or for
  corruption.
- `wal.rec` is a small marker written after validation and before the
  repair, recording the clean prefix length and the discarded count. A
  repair interrupted mid-copy is simply repeated on reopen, and the marker
  keeps `discarded` stable across reopens and repeated recoveries until the
  next successful commit closes the epoch.

Only the final record may be incomplete. Any incomplete record elsewhere,
a length out of bounds, unparseable content, or a duplicate/regressing
sequence is corruption: recovery raises `wal_store.CorruptLogError`
(a subclass of `ValueError`) and stops without applying or removing
anything.

The command line `recover` prints the report as one compact JSON line with
the same key order and a trailing newline, e.g.
`{"applied":2,"discarded":0,"seq":1}`. Discarding a torn tail is not an
error and the exit code is `0`; corruption prints one explanatory line to
standard error and exits `3` without printing the JSON line.

## Compaction

`compact()` reclaims history without sacrificing any committed state. When
it finishes, the log contains exactly the live committed key/values: one
put frame per currently committed key, in sorted key order, followed by a
base commit marker that carries the pre-compaction sequence. Deleted keys
are gone for good — a deleted key can never reappear — and overwritten keys
keep only their final value. The durable sequence number is unchanged, so
the next `commit()` writes `seq + 1`; every commit advances, including an
empty one, and subsequent commits continue the strict sequence as if no
rewrite had happened. The empty committed state
(including "everything was deleted") compacts to an empty log.

`compact()` returns the same three-field report shape as `recover()`:
`applied` is the number of live puts the new log contains, `discarded` is
always `0` and `seq` is the preserved sequence. Uncommitted session changes
make it raise `ValueError`; commit or discard them first.

Compaction is a kill-safe, idempotent convergence like recovery. The new
image is assembled in memory and durably staged as the `wal.cmp` sidecar
(an atomically replaced complete file, never an in-place edit), then
published in two atomic steps — `wal.ckp` first and `wal.log` second —
before the staging file is removed. A process killed at any point, any
number of times, leaves a store that finishes the identical publish on the
next open: the recovered state is exactly the last committed state, the
sequence never regresses and the resulting log/sidecar bytes are
byte-identical to one uninterrupted compaction. Repeating compaction on an
already compact store produces the same bytes.

Live read-only stores are unaffected: they keep serving the complete
snapshot they pinned before, during and after compaction (it lands on the
other half of the same log-versus-checkpoint pair readers already choose
between), while fresh readers open the compacted snapshot. No reader ever
sees a mix of old and new bytes, a half-written file, or content whose
space was reclaimed; killing a reader does not disturb compaction and
killing the compactor does not disturb a reader. Compaction introduces no
new limits beyond the existing single-writer rule, and directories written
by older versions compact directly with no conversion step.

## Tests

    python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

## Limits

One writer at a time; no cross-process locking.
Values are bytes; encoding is the caller concern.
No replication; compaction is a writer-initiated rewrite, not background
garbage collection.

189	    does not disturb it. The cursor is an iterator; it is also a context
190	    manager, and ``close()`` releases the snapshot early. Reading from a
191	    closed cursor raises ``ValueError``.
192	
193	    :meth:`token` serialises the current position into an opaque ``bytes``
194	    token naming the pinned snapshot, the scan range and the next position.
195	    ``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in this process or in a freshly opened
196	    store -- continues the identical scan from that position.
197	    """
198	
199	    def __init__(self, items, lo_idx=0, hi_idx=None, pos=None, seq=0,
200	                 lo=None, hi=None, publisher=None):
201	        # ``items`` is the materialised snapshot: (key, value) pairs already
202	        # sorted by the keys' raw UTF-8 bytes. The visible window is
203	        # [lo_idx, hi_idx) and the next position starts at ``pos``.
204	        self._items = items
205	        self._lo_idx = lo_idx
206	        self._hi_idx = len(items) if hi_idx is None else hi_idx
207	        self._pos = lo_idx if pos is None else pos
208	        self._seq = seq
209	        self._lo = lo
210	        self._hi = hi
211	        # Writer-only callback durably publishing the pinned snapshot so a
212	        # minted token survives compaction and reclamation; ``None`` on
213	        # read-only stores, which never create or modify any file.
214	        self._publisher = publisher
215	        self._sid = None
216	        self._box = None
217	        self._closed = False
218	
219	    def __iter__(self) -> "ScanCursor":
220	        return self
221	
222	    def __next__(self):
223	        if self._closed:
224	            raise ValueError("scan cursor is closed")
225	        if self._pos >= self._hi_idx:
226	            raise StopIteration
227	        item = self._items[self._pos]
228	        self._pos += 1
229	        return item
230	
231	    def token(self) -> bytes:
232	        """Serialise the current position into an opaque scan token.
233	
234	        The returned ``bytes`` name the pinned snapshot (its durable
235	        sequence number and content identity), the scan range and the next
236	        position. Feeding the token to ``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in this
237	        process or in a freshly opened store, writer or read-only -- opens
238	        a cursor that continues the same range from the same position over
239	        the same pinned snapshot, byte-identical to the tail of this scan.
240	
241	        Token bytes are platform-independent and deterministic: the same
242	        snapshot at the same position always mints the same token. On a
243	        writer store minting also publishes the pinned snapshot as an
244	        immutable sidecar so the token survives compaction and reclamation
245	        of the old log space; a read-only store never writes anything.
246	        """
247	        if self._closed:
248	            raise ValueError("scan cursor is closed")
249	        if self._sid is None:
250	            self._sid = _snapshot_id(self._items)
251	        if self._publisher is not None:
252	            self._publisher(self._seq, self._sid, self._items)
253	        self._box = _register_snapshot(self._seq, self._sid, self._items)
254	        return _encode_token(self._seq, self._sid, self._lo, self._hi,
255	                             self._pos)
256	
257	    def mark(self) -> bytes:
258	        """Alias for :meth:`token`."""
259	        return self.token()
260	
261	    @property
262	    def closed(self) -> bool:
263	        return self._closed
264	
265	    def close(self) -> None:
266	        self._items = []
267	        self._box = None
268	        self._closed = True
269	
270	    def __enter__(self) -> "ScanCursor":
271	        return self
272	
273	    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) -> None:
274	        self.close()

279	_MARKER_NAME = "wal.rec"
280	_COMPACT_NAME = "wal.cmp"

282	_MAGIC = b"WAL2"
283	_PREFIX = 12  # 4 bytes magic + 8 bytes payload length
284	_HEADER = 16   # prefix + 4 bytes crc32 of the prefix
285	_TRAILER = 4   # crc32 of the payload
286	_MAX_PAYLOAD = 1 << 40
287	
288	_OP_PUT = "p"
289	_OP_DELETE = "d"
290	_OP_RANGE = "r"
291	_OP_COMMIT = "c"
292	_OP_BASE = "b"
293	_COMMIT_OPS = (_OP_COMMIT, _OP_BASE)

295	
296	# Pinned-snapshot sidecars (``wal.s<seq>.<id>``) and scan tokens. A token
297	# is an opaque, platform-independent byte string: magic, the snapshot's
298	# durable sequence, its 32-byte content identity, the optional range
299	# endpoints, the next position and a checksum -- all integers big-endian,
300	# so the same snapshot and position mint byte-identical tokens everywhere.
301	_TOKEN_MAGIC = b"WST1"
302	_SNAPSHOT_PREFIX = "wal.s"
303	_EMPTY_SNAPSHOT_ID = hashlib.sha256(b"").digest()

306	def _snapshot_image(items) -> bytes:
307	    """Canonical byte image of a committed snapshot: one put frame per key.
308	
309	    ``items`` must already be sorted by the keys' raw UTF-8 bytes. The
310	    image uses the same deterministic framing as the log, so it is
311	    identical on every platform for the same snapshot.
312	    """
313	    return b"".join(_encode_frame(_OP_PUT, value, key=key)
314	                    for key, value in items)

318	    """Content identity of a committed snapshot (32 raw bytes)."""
319	    return hashlib.sha256(_snapshot_image(items)).digest()

322	def _encode_token(seq: int, sid: bytes, lo: bytes | None,
323	                  hi: bytes | None, pos: int) -> bytes:
324	    """Serialise a scan position; the exact inverse of :func:`_decode_token`."""
325	    flags = (1 if lo is not None else 0) | (2 if hi is not None else 0)
326	    parts = [_TOKEN_MAGIC, seq.to_bytes(8, "big"), sid, bytes((flags,))]
327	    for bound in (lo, hi):
328	        raw = bound if bound is not None else b""
329	        parts.append(len(raw).to_bytes(4, "big"))
330	        parts.append(raw)
331	    parts.append(pos.to_bytes(8, "big"))
332	    body = b"".join(parts)
333	    return body + zlib.crc32(body).to_bytes(4, "big")

336	def _decode_token(tok: bytes):
337	    """Parse a scan token into ``(seq, sid, lo, hi, pos)``.
338	
339	    Every malformation -- wrong magic, truncation, trailing garbage, a
340	    checksum mismatch, unknown flags, a hidden endpoint or a reversed
341	    range -- raises ``ValueError``; nothing is guessed or repaired.
342	    """
343	    if len(tok) < 4 + 8 + 32 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 8 + 4:
344	        raise ValueError("not a scan token")
345	    if tok[:4] != _TOKEN_MAGIC:
346	        raise ValueError("not a scan token")
347	    if int.from_bytes(tok[-4:], "big") != zlib.crc32(tok[:-4]):
348	        raise ValueError("scan token checksum mismatch")
349	    off = 4
350	    seq = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 8], "big")
351	    off += 8
352	    sid = tok[off:off + 32]
353	    off += 32
354	    flags = tok[off]
355	    off += 1
356	    if flags & ~0x03:
357	        raise ValueError("scan token carries unknown flags")
358	    bounds = []
359	    for present in (flags & 1, flags & 2):
360	        if off + 4 > len(tok) - 4:
361	            raise ValueError("scan token is truncated")
362	        size = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 4], "big")
363	        off += 4
364	        if off + size > len(tok) - 4:
365	            raise ValueError("scan token is truncated")
366	        if not present and size != 0:
367	            raise ValueError("scan token carries a hidden endpoint")
368	        bounds.append(tok[off:off + size] if present else None)
369	        off += size
370	    if off + 8 != len(tok) - 4:
371	        raise ValueError("scan token length mismatch")
372	    pos = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 8], "big")
373	    lo, hi = bounds
374	    if lo is not None and hi is not None and lo > hi:
375	        raise ValueError("scan token range is reversed")
376	    return seq, sid, lo, hi, pos

380	    """Strong box around a materialised snapshot for the process registry."""

382	    __slots__ = ("items", "__weakref__")

388	# (seq, snapshot id) -> _SnapshotBox, held weakly: an entry lives only
389	# while some live cursor or resolver references it, so pinned history
390	# never accumulates in memory. It lets a token minted in this process
391	# resolve without touching disk; every other path resolves from the
392	# durable files.
393	_SNAPSHOTS: "weakref.WeakValueDictionary" = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()

397	    key = (seq, sid)
398	    box = _SNAPSHOTS.get(key)
399	    if box is None:
400	        box = _SnapshotBox(items)
401	        _SNAPSHOTS[key] = box
402	    return box

411	def _range_bounds_from_meta(meta) -> tuple[bytes | None, bytes | None]:
412	    """Decode and validate the two endpoints of a range tombstone frame.
413	
414	    Returns their raw UTF-8 bytes, ``None`` for a ``null`` (unbounded)
415	    side. Missing, mistyped or unencodable endpoints are corruption.
416	    """
417	    if not isinstance(meta, dict):
418	        raise CorruptLogError(f"invalid range tombstone metadata: {meta!r}")
419	    if "s" not in meta or "e" not in meta:
420	        raise CorruptLogError(
421	            f"range tombstone is missing an endpoint: {meta!r}")
422	    lo = meta.get("s")
423	    hi = meta.get("e")
424	    for endpoint in (lo, hi):
425	        if endpoint is not None and not isinstance(endpoint, str):
426	            raise CorruptLogError(
427	                f"invalid range tombstone endpoint: {meta!r}")
428	    try:
429	        lo_b = lo.encode("utf-8") if lo is not None else None
430	        hi_b = hi.encode("utf-8") if hi is not None else None
431	    except (UnicodeEncodeError, AttributeError):
432	        raise CorruptLogError(
433	            f"invalid range tombstone endpoint: {meta!r}")
434	    return lo_b, hi_b

438	                  hi: bytes | None) -> bool:
439	    """Half-open bytewise membership: ``lo <= key < hi``, null unbounded."""
440	    if lo is not None and key_bytes < lo:
441	        return False
442	    if hi is not None and key_bytes >= hi:
443	        return False
444	    return True

447	def _encode_frame(op: str, value: bytes = b"", key: str | None = None,
448	                  seq: int | None = None, start: str | None = None,
449	                  end: str | None = None) -> bytes:
450	    meta: dict[str, object] = {"t": op}
451	    if op == _OP_RANGE:
452	        # Both endpoints are always carried; null leaves that side open.
453	        meta["s"] = start
454	        meta["e"] = end
455	    else:
456	        if key is not None:
457	            meta["k"] = key
458	        if seq is not None:
459	            meta["s"] = seq
460	    head = json.dumps(meta, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")
461	    payload = head + b"\n" + value
462	    prefix = _MAGIC + len(payload).to_bytes(8, "big")
463	    header = prefix + zlib.crc32(prefix).to_bytes(4, "big")
464	    return header + payload + zlib.crc32(payload).to_bytes(4, "big")

467	def _iter_frames(f):
468	    """Scan an open binary log file from position 0.
469	
470	    For every intact frame yields
471	    ``("frame", meta, value, start, end)``. Scanning stops with either no
472	    terminal event (clean EOF), ``("torn", start)`` for a single incomplete
473	    final frame, or ``("invalid", start)`` for a frame that fails framing,
474	    header/payload checksum or metadata parsing. With the header checksum a
475	    partial header that borrows bytes from a following record cannot survive,
476	    so a short read landing exactly at EOF is reliably the one unfinished
477	    record a single writer was appending when it died; bytes left beyond such
478	    a read instead make it corruption.
479	    """
480	    f.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
481	    eof = f.tell()
482	    f.seek(0)
483	    while True:
484	        start = f.tell()
485	        header = f.read(_HEADER)
486	        if not header:
487	            return
488	        if len(header) < _HEADER:
489	            # Trailing bytes of a frame header are a torn tail only when
490	            # nothing follows them; a gap anywhere else is corruption.
491	            yield (("torn", start) if f.tell() == eof
492	                   else ("invalid", start))
493	            return
494	        if header[:4] != _MAGIC:
495	            yield "invalid", start
496	            return
497	        if int.from_bytes(header[_PREFIX:], "big") != zlib.crc32(
498	                header[:_PREFIX]):
499	            yield "invalid", start
500	            return
501	        length = int.from_bytes(header[4:_PREFIX], "big")
502	        if length > _MAX_PAYLOAD:
503	            yield "invalid", start
504	            return
505	        payload = f.read(length)
506	        checksum = f.read(_TRAILER)
507	        if len(payload) < length or len(checksum) < _TRAILER:
508	            # Only the single final record may be incomplete.
509	            yield (("torn", start) if f.tell() == eof
510	                   else ("invalid", start))
511	            return
512	        if int.from_bytes(checksum, "big") != zlib.crc32(payload):
513	            yield "invalid", start
514	            return
515	        newline = payload.find(b"\n")
516	        if newline < 0:
517	            yield "invalid", start
518	            return
519	        try:
520	            meta = json.loads(payload[:newline])
521	        except (ValueError, UnicodeDecodeError):
522	            yield "invalid", start
523	            return
524	        if not isinstance(meta, dict) or not isinstance(meta.get("t"), str):
525	            yield "invalid", start
526	            return
527	        yield "frame", meta, payload[newline + 1:], start, f.tell()

530	def _fsync_dir(path: str) -> None:
531	    """Fsync a directory so a nearby rename/unlink is durable.
532	
533	    Windows cannot open directories for fsync and raises ``PermissionError``
534	    (access denied); directory entries there are made durable by the file's
535	    own flush-on-rename, so skipping the directory fsync keeps store creation
536	    working everywhere. Other platforms occasionally refuse the directory
537	    open or the fsync (restrictive mounts, virtualised FSes); that is
538	    likewise best-effort -- the file's own fsync is what carries the data.
539	    Any refusal, whatever ``OSError`` form it takes, is absorbed: a rejected
540	    directory sync never aborts store creation, a commit or a compaction,
541	    and never affects later writes.
542	    """
543	    if sys.platform == "win32":
544	        return
545	    try:
546	        fd = os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY)
547	    except OSError:
548	        return
549	    try:
550	        try:
551	            os.fsync(fd)
552	        except OSError:
553	            # Some non-Windows mounts reject directory fsync, in any form.
554	            pass
555	    finally:
556	        os.close(fd)

565	def inject_tear(source, destination, offset):
566	    """Copy a log cut at exactly ``offset`` bytes, for bytewise verification.
567	
568	    Produces ``destination`` containing the first ``offset`` bytes of
569	    ``source`` -- a replica of a process killed precisely when the write had
570	    reached that byte offset. The source file is never modified. Either path
571	    argument may be a store directory, in which case its ``wal.log`` is used.
572	
573	    ``offset`` must satisfy ``0 <= offset <= len(source)``; a negative or
574	    past-the-end offset raises ``IndexError``. The full-length copy
575	    (``offset == len(source)``) is the clean control case.
576	
577	    Verification aid only; the normal write path never calls this.
578	    """
579	    if not isinstance(offset, int) or isinstance(offset, bool):
580	        raise TypeError("offset must be an integer byte offset")
581	
582	    src = os.path.join(source, LOG_NAME) if os.path.isdir(source) else source
583	    dst = (os.path.join(destination, LOG_NAME)
584	           if os.path.isdir(destination) else destination)
585	
586	    size = os.path.getsize(src)
587	    if offset < 0 or offset > size:
588	        raise IndexError(
589	            f"tear offset {offset} out of range for log of {size} bytes")
590	    if os.path.abspath(src) == os.path.abspath(dst):
591	        raise ValueError("tear destination must differ from the source log")
592	
593	    remaining = offset
594	    with open(src, "rb") as fsrc, open(dst, "wb") as fdst:
595	        while remaining:
596	            chunk = fsrc.read(min(remaining, 1 << 20))
597	            if not chunk:  # pragma: no cover - size came from the same file
598	                raise IndexError("source log shrank while copying")
599	            fdst.write(chunk)
600	            remaining -= len(chunk)
601	        fdst.truncate(offset)
602	        os.fsync(fdst.fileno())
603	    return dst

606	class Store:
607	    """A single-writer key value store backed by an append-only log.
608	
609	    ``path`` must be an existing store directory; the log file inside it is
610	    created on first use. Opening a missing directory raises
611	    ``FileNotFoundError`` and opening a path that is not a directory raises
612	    ``OSError``.
613	
614	    With ``read_only=True`` the store is opened purely for reading. No file
615	    is ever created or modified, and no lock is taken: any number of
616	    read-only processes may coexist with the one writer. The reader pins the
617	    committed snapshot current at open time -- the highest committed prefix
618	    of ``wal.log`` or of the atomically replaced ``wal.ckp`` sidecar --
619	    scans it once, and serves every ``get`` from that in-memory index. The
620	    snapshot is independent of the log's later history, so a read never
621	    replays the log and cannot block the writer, and uncommitted bytes, a
622	    half-written commit, a torn record or a half-finished rebuild are never
623	    visible. ``put``, ``delete`` (including its range form),
624	    ``delete_range``, ``commit``, ``recover`` and ``compact``
625	    are rejected on a read-only store; ``stats`` reports the pinned
626	    snapshot.
627	
628	    ``scan(start, end)`` -- on either open form -- returns a
629	    :class:`ScanCursor` over the complete committed snapshot pinned at the
630	    moment of the call, yielding ``(key, value)`` pairs in bytewise key
631	    order from ``start`` (inclusive) to ``end`` (exclusive); a ``None``
632	    endpoint leaves that side unbounded. Uncommitted session changes of a
633	    writer are not part of the snapshot, and neither are they visible to
634	    ``get``: single-key reads see the last committed snapshot too. The
635	    cursor reads from memory only: it never touches the log, takes no lock,
636	    and is unaffected by later commits, compaction, recovery or the store
637	    closing. ``scan(token=...)`` instead resumes the pinned scan a token
638	    from :meth:`ScanCursor.token` belongs to, from its recorded position.
639	    """
640	
641	    def __init__(self, path: str, read_only: bool = False):
642	        self._dir = path
643	        self._path = os.path.join(path, LOG_NAME)
644	        self._ckp_path = os.path.join(path, _CHECKPOINT_NAME)
645	        self._marker_path = os.path.join(path, _MARKER_NAME)
646	        self._cmp_path = os.path.join(path, _COMPACT_NAME)
647	        self._read_only = read_only
648	
649	        # Recovery needs a directory to replay; a missing target is an error
650	        # at open time, not an implicit create.
651	        if not os.path.exists(path):
652	            raise FileNotFoundError(
653	                f"store directory does not exist: {path!r}")
654	        if not os.path.isdir(path):
655	            raise OSError(f"store path is not a directory: {path!r}")
656	
657	        self._data: dict[str, bytes] = {}
658	        self._seq = 0
659	        self._entries = 0
660	        self._pending = 0
661	        self._closed = False
662	        self._corrupt = False
663	        # Committed value of each key this session has touched since the
664	        # last commit (None when the key was absent); lets a scan pin the
665	        # committed snapshot without replaying the log.
666	        self._touched: dict[str, bytes | None] = {}
667	        # Torn records dropped in this recovery epoch; wal.rec carries it
668	        # across processes until the next commit.
669	        self._discarded = 0
670	
671	        if read_only:
672	            # A read-only open holds no writable fd and never takes a lock;
673	            # leave the writer fd slot unset for clarity.
674	            self._fd = -1
675	            self._open_read_only()
676	            return
677	
678	        log_created = not os.path.exists(self._path)
679	        self._fd = os.open(self._path,
680	                           os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_APPEND | _O_BINARY,
681	                           0o644)
682	        if log_created:
683	            os.fsync(self._fd)
684	            _fsync_dir(path)
685	
686	        self._converge_on_open()
687	
688	    # -- log scanning and validation --------------------------------------
689	
690	    def _read_log(self, path=None):
691	        frames = []
692	        terminal = None
693	        with open(path or self._path, "rb") as f:
694	            for event in _iter_frames(f):
695	                if event[0] == "frame":
696	                    _, meta, value, start, end = event
697	                    frames.append((meta, value, start, end))
698	                else:
699	                    terminal = event
700	        return frames, terminal
701	
702	    @staticmethod
703	    def _validate(frames, terminal):
704	        """Validate every frame and the strictly increasing commit sequence.
705	
706	        Returns ``(committed_end, last_seq)`` -- the byte offset just past
707	        the last commit marker and its sequence number. An ``"invalid"``
708	        terminal is corruption and raises ``CorruptLogError``; a ``"torn"``
709	        terminal is left for the caller, which decides from the durable
710	        checkpoint whether it is a tail to discard or a gash to restore.
711	
712	        A compacted image starts with a base commit marker (``"b"``) that
713	        carries the pre-compaction sequence: it must be the first commit
714	        marker in the file, it establishes the expected sequence at
715	        ``seq + 1`` and no second base marker may ever follow. An ordinary
716	        first commit must still be sequence 1.
717	        """
718	        expected_seq = 1
719	        last_seq = 0
720	        committed_end = 0
721	        for meta, _value, _start, end in frames:
722	            op = meta.get("t")
723	            if op in (_OP_PUT, _OP_DELETE):
724	                key = meta.get("k")
725	                if not isinstance(key, str) or key == "":
726	                    raise CorruptLogError(
727	                        f"invalid frame metadata: {meta!r}")
728	            elif op == _OP_RANGE:
729	                # Both endpoints must be present and be a string or null;
730	                # the bounds must not be reversed.
731	                lo, hi = _range_bounds_from_meta(meta)
732	                if lo is not None and hi is not None and lo > hi:
733	                    raise CorruptLogError(
734	                        f"range tombstone endpoints out of order: {meta!r}")
735	            elif op == _OP_BASE:
736	                seq = meta.get("s")
737	                if not isinstance(seq, int) or isinstance(seq, bool):
738	                    raise CorruptLogError(
739	                        f"invalid base commit marker: {meta!r}")
740	                if last_seq != 0:
741	                    raise CorruptLogError(
742	                        "base commit must be the first commit marker")
743	                if seq < 1:
744	                    raise CorruptLogError(
745	                        f"base commit sequence {seq} out of order")
746	                last_seq = seq
747	                expected_seq = seq + 1
748	                committed_end = end
749	            elif op == _OP_COMMIT:
750	                seq = meta.get("s")
751	                if not isinstance(seq, int) or isinstance(seq, bool):
752	                    raise CorruptLogError(
753	                        f"invalid commit marker: {meta!r}")
754	                if seq != expected_seq:

958	    def _build_compact_image(self, seq: int) -> tuple[bytes, int]:

960

962	        commit marker carrying the pre-compaction sequence. The empty state
963	        at seq 0 is an empty image rather than a zero-sequence marker.
964	        """

966	            return b"", 0

968	                 for key, value in sorted(self._data.items())]
969	        parts.append(_encode_frame(_OP_BASE, seq=seq))

976	        byte content, or ``None`` when the sidecar is absent. The image must
977	        be a clean file ending exactly on a base commit marker, preceded only
978	        by put frames with strictly increasing keys; anything else is
979	        corruption of the crash-convergence machinery, never a discardable
980	        tail (the sidecar is always atomically replaced, never written in
981	        place).
982	        """

984	            f = open(self._cmp_path, "rb")
985	        except FileNotFoundError:

1430	    def scan(self, start: str | None = None, end: str | None = None,
1431	             *, token: bytes | None = None,
1432	             resume: bytes | None = None) -> ScanCursor:
1433	        """Open an ordered cursor over the pinned committed snapshot.
1434	
1435	        The cursor yields ``(key, value)`` pairs in bytewise key order --
1436	        keys compared by their raw UTF-8 bytes, values returned as the exact
1437	        stored bytes -- covering ``start`` (inclusive) through ``end``
1438	        (exclusive). A ``None`` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so
1439	        ``scan()`` walks the whole snapshot. Keys that only ever appeared in
1440	        delete records or inside a deleted range are absent, a key
1441	        overwritten any number of times yields only its last committed
1442	        value, and empty values scan like any other. A writer's uncommitted
1443	        session changes are not part of the snapshot; a read-only store
1444	        scans the snapshot it pinned at open.
1445	
1446	        With ``token`` (alias ``resume``) the call instead continues the
1447	        scan a :meth:`ScanCursor.token` token belongs to: the token names
1448	        its pinned snapshot, range and position, and the returned cursor
1449	        yields exactly the tail of that original scan -- in this process or
1450	        in a freshly opened store, across later commits, compaction, crash
1451	        recovery and reclamation of the old log space. Endpoints must not
1452	        accompany a token (the token carries its range). A token that is
1453	        forged, truncated, corrupted, out of range or names a snapshot this
1454	        store does not hold raises ``ValueError``; a non-bytes token raises
1455	        ``TypeError``.
1456	
1457	        The snapshot is materialised once, here, so the cursor is
1458	        independent of later commits, compaction, crash recovery and log
1459	        space reclamation, and its cost is independent of the log's history
1460	        length. A ``start`` that sorts after ``end`` raises ``ValueError``,
1461	        as does reading from the cursor after it is closed.
1462	        """

1464	        if token is not None and resume is not None:
1465	            raise ValueError("pass only one scan token")
1466	        tok = token if token is not None else resume
1467	        if tok is not None:
1468	            if start is not None or end is not None:
1469	                raise ValueError(
1470	                    "range endpoints must not accompany a scan token")
1471	            return self._resume_scan(tok)
1472	        lo, hi = self._check_range(start, end)
1473	
1474	        data = self._ro_index if self._read_only else self._committed_view()
1475	        seq = self._ro_seq if self._read_only else self._seq
1476	        items = self._sorted_snapshot_items(data)
1477	        lo_idx, hi_idx = self._range_window(items, lo, hi)

1486	        return sorted(
1487	            ((key, bytes(value)) for key, value in data.items()),

1490	    @staticmethod

1492	        """Index window of the half-open bytewise range in sorted items."""
1493	        keys = [key.encode("utf-8") for key, _value in items]
1494	        lo_idx = bisect.bisect_left(keys, lo) if lo is not None else 0
1495	        hi_idx = (bisect.bisect_left(keys, hi) if hi is not None
1496	                  else len(items))

1542	    def _read_snapshot_blob(self, seq: int, sid: bytes):
1543	        """Load and verify a published snapshot sidecar; ``None`` if absent.

1548	        mismatched sidecar is corruption of the snapshot machinery, never
1549	        silently skipped.
1550	        """

1676	    def delete(self, key: str | None, end: str | None = None) -> None:

1696	    def delete_range(self, start: str | None = None,

1698	        """Record a range tombstone deleting every committed key in range.

1700	        Every key whose raw UTF-8 bytes sort at or after ``start`` and
1701	        strictly before ``end`` is deleted: half-open, bytewise, exactly the
1702	        range convention of :meth:`scan`. A ``None`` endpoint leaves that
1703	        side unbounded, so ``delete_range()`` deletes the whole store and
1704	        ``delete_range("a", "a")`` deletes nothing. Deleting a range, then
1705	        writing keys inside it, keeps those new values -- the tombstone is
1706	        fixed to the state before it -- and keys that were deleted are never
1707	        resurrected by recovery or compaction.
1708	
1709	        Like :meth:`delete` the change is staged in this session and becomes
1710	        durable only at the next :meth:`commit`; until then it is invisible
1711	        to scans, single-key reads of the committed snapshot and read-only
1712	        stores, and a crash simply discards it. A ``start`` sorting after
1713	        ``end`` raises ``ValueError`` (the same check ``scan`` uses) and a
1714	        non-string endpoint raises ``TypeError``.
1715	        """
1716	        self._ensure_writable()
1717	        lo, hi = self._check_range(start, end)
1718	
1719	        _write_all(self._fd, _encode_frame(_OP_RANGE, start=start, end=end))
1720	
1721	        # Fold the tombstone into the live session view the same way a
1722	        # single delete folds its key; each committed key it covers
1723	        # remembers its pre-session value so a scan can still reconstruct
1724	        # the untouched committed snapshot before commit.

1726	                   if _key_in_range(key.encode("utf-8"), lo, hi)]

1728	            if key not in self._touched:
1729	                self._touched[key] = self._data.get(key)

1732	        self._entries += 1

1734	    def commit(self) -> int:

1746	        # new restorable prefix, then close the recovery epoch.

1751	        self._pending = 0
1752	        self._touched = {}
1753	        self._entries += 1
1754	        self._discarded = 0

1760	        # temp file.

1767	    def recover(self) -> dict:
1768	        """Replay the log and return ``{"applied", "discarded", "seq"}``.
1769	
1770	        ``applied`` counts the committed mutation records replayed (puts,
1771	        deletes and range tombstones), ``discarded`` is 1 when a single
1772	        torn final record was dropped (0 otherwise) and ``seq`` is the
1773	        durable sequence number after recovery. Raises
1774	        ``CorruptLogError`` (a ``ValueError``) if the log is corrupt;
1775	        nothing is applied or truncated in that case.
1776	
1777	        Recovery is idempotent and kill-safe: interrupting it any number of
1778	        times and rerunning converges to the same state and the same report
1779	        as one clean recovery, and the next commit always uses ``seq + 1``.
1780	        """
1781	        self._ensure_open()
1782	        if self._read_only:
1783	            raise ValueError("cannot recover a store opened read-only")
1784	        if self._pending:
1785	            raise ValueError(
1786	                "cannot recover with uncommitted changes in this session")
1787	
1788	        # Re-validate and re-converge; a genuinely corrupt log raises here
1789	        # before anything is applied or removed.
1790	        frames, discarded = self._converge()
1791	
1792	        state, applied = self._replay(frames)
1793	        seq = self._last_seq(frames)
1794	        self._data = state
1795	        self._seq = seq
1796	        self._entries = len(frames)
1797	        self._pending = 0
1798	        self._touched = {}
1799	        self._discarded = discarded
1800	        self._corrupt = False
1801	        return {"applied": applied, "discarded": discarded, "seq": seq}

1803	    def compact(self) -> dict:

1807	        per live key (sorted by key) followed by a base commit marker that
1808	        carries the pre-compaction sequence number. Deleted keys are gone for
1809	        good, the durable sequence keeps its value (the next commit is
1810	        ``seq + 1``) and the old log/checkpoint space is reclaimed. The
1811	        empty committed state compacts to an empty log.

1813	        Returns the same three-field report shape as :meth:`recover` for the
1814	        compacted log: ``applied`` is the live puts it now contains,
1815	        ``discarded`` is always 0 and ``seq`` is the preserved sequence.
1816	
1817	        Uncommitted session changes are rejected (``ValueError``). The image
1818	        is staged as a complete sidecar and published by two atomic
1819	        renames, so a kill at any byte/step -- including a kill repeated any
1820	        number of times -- leaves a state the next open converges by simply
1821	        finishing the same publish, byte-identical to one clean compaction.
1822	        Live read-only stores keep pinning their old complete snapshots
1823	        throughout; compaction never waits on or is disturbed by them.
1824	        """
1825	        self._ensure_writable()
1826	        if self._pending:
1827	            raise ValueError(
1828	                "cannot compact with uncommitted changes in this session")
1829	
1830	        # Settle any crash remnant (including an interrupted compaction)
1831	        # before snapshotting the committed state.
1832	        frames, discarded = self._converge()
1833	        state, _applied = self._replay(frames)
1834	        seq = self._last_seq(frames)
1835	        self._data = state
1836	        self._seq = seq
1837	        self._entries = len(frames)
1838	        self._pending = 0
1839	        self._touched = {}
1840	        self._discarded = discarded

"""Write-ahead log key value store.

Every mutation is first appended to a framed log. A commit marker is the
only thing that advances the durable sequence number, and every
``commit()`` writes one -- including an empty commit with nothing pending,
which advances the sequence by exactly one like any other commit. When a
store is opened, any tail that was never committed (including a record
torn by a hard kill) is discarded, so recovery always yields exactly the
committed state. Single-key reads and scans of a writer both see only the
last committed snapshot; uncommitted session changes are invisible to
either.

Only the very last log record may be incomplete: a process killed while
appending leaves at most one torn record, which is dropped without being
applied. Any other framing failure -- a truncated record in the middle, a
length field out of bounds, unparseable content, or a duplicate/regressing
commit sequence -- is corruption, and recovery raises ``CorruptLogError``
without touching the store.

Recovery itself may be killed at any point, any number of times. Two small
sidecar files in the store directory, both maintained below the write path,
make the convergence protocol kill-safe and its report stable:

``wal.ckp``
    A byte-for-byte copy of the log prefix ending at the most recent commit
    marker, replaced atomically (temp file, fsync, rename, directory fsync)
    only after that commit frame is durable. A log torn at *any* offset --
    even offset 0, or inside the committed prefix -- is rebuilt from it, so
    the durable sequence number never regresses. It is also the published
    snapshot read-only processes pin (see below).

``wal.rec``
    A recovery marker written only after a log needing repair has passed
    full validation and only *before* the atomic rebuild starts. It records
    the clean prefix length and whether a torn record was discarded. Its
    presence makes a rebuild interrupted mid-copy converge on reopen (the
    rebuild is simply repeated) and keeps the reported ``discarded`` count
    stable across reopens and repeated recoveries. It is removed by the next
    successful commit.

Range scans (``Store.scan(start, end)``) open an ordered read-only cursor
over the complete committed snapshot pinned at the moment the cursor is
opened. The cursor yields ``(key, value)`` pairs in bytewise key order --
keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes, with no encoding conversion -- from
``start`` (inclusive) to ``end`` (exclusive); a ``None`` endpoint leaves
that side unbounded. Keys that only ever appear in delete records never
show up, a key overwritten many times yields only its last committed value,
and empty values scan like any other. The snapshot is materialised once
when the cursor opens, so commits, compaction or crash recovery during the
scan never change it, reclaiming the old log space cannot break it, and the
cost of a scan is independent of how long the log's history is. A reversed
range (``start`` after ``end``) and any read from a closed cursor raise
``ValueError``.

A cursor's position serialises into an opaque ``bytes`` token via
``ScanCursor.token()``. The token names the pinned snapshot -- its durable
sequence number and a content identity over the snapshot's canonical image
-- together with the scan range and the next position. Passing it back as
``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in the same process or in a freshly opened
store, writer or read-only -- continues the identical range from the
identical position over the identical snapshot, so the resumed stream is
byte-for-byte the tail of the original scan. Tokens stay valid across
later commits, compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log
space: a writer durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an immutable
``wal.s<seq>.<id>`` sidecar when a token is minted, and snapshots that
were never published still resolve from the committed log prefix or the
checkpoint. Deleted keys -- including keys covered by range tombstones
